scenario: AITA for deleting my stepbrothers profile on my Nintendo switch? | At the beginning of the school year I had to watch my stepbrother for a week while my dad and his mom went on a trip to help out her parents with something. Brought my switch with me because my school is more than an hour away and I wanted something to do on the train during my commute everyday. My stepbrother wanted to play on it. Him being so into it actually turned into a big help to distract him while I studied, so I made a new profile on it for him so he wouldn’t mess up my saves. When I got back to school I eventually got annoyed with having to click on my profile each time I started a game and each time I went to the eshop. So I just deleted his profile. So, this early this morning I got on the train to go to my dads for thanksgiving. I usually go home to my moms, but she and my stepdad are going to see his family and Im not up for going plane trip. Anyway I brought my switch again for the train ride. Just a little while ago my stepbrother picked it up to start playing and came into the kitchen, where I was talking with my dad, freaking out because his Zelda save was gone and he wanted me to help him fix it. When I told him I deleted it he started crying. Like not full on crying, but his eyes were watery a little and red. Now he’s holed up in his room. My dad thinks it was mean of me to delete it because I know my stepbrother was enjoying playing it. I didn’t think it was a big deal since I usually never bring my switch over when I visit.

Here’s how they might influence your perspective and character over time: ### **1. Developing Resilience and Adaptability** - **Handling chaos with grace**: Juggling multiple demands teaches you to pivot quickly, problem-solve under pressure, and stay calm when things don’t go as planned. This can foster a sense of inner strength and resourcefulness. - **Embracing imperfection**: No day goes perfectly, and learning to adapt to unexpected changes (a missed nap, a forgotten lunch, a last-minute doctor’s appointment) can make you more resilient to stress in other areas of life. ### **2. Cultivating Empathy and Perspective-Taking** - **Seeing the world through others’ eyes**: Constantly checking in with your children’s needs (and maybe even your partner’s) can deepen your ability to understand and care for others’ emotions. This empathy often extends beyond your family to friends, colleagues, or even strangers. - **Gratitude for small joys**: When you’re hyper-aware of what’s *missing* (a full stomach, a clean diaper, a quiet moment), you might also become more attuned to the little things that *do* go right—a warm hug, a shared laugh, a sunset. This can foster a more appreciative outlook. ### **3. Strengthening Time Management and Prioritization** - **Learning to say "no" (or "not now")**: Balancing responsibilities forces you to set boundaries, delegate, or accept help. This can translate into healthier work-life balance, clearer goals, and less guilt about trade-offs. - **Finding efficiency in chaos**: Over time, you might develop a "mother’s intuition" for streamlining tasks (meal prepping, batching chores, or using tools like shared calendars). This self-awareness is a superpower in relationships and personal well-being. - **Balancing care for self and others**: The best mothers (and people) often learn to fill their own cup so they can pour into others. This can lead to healthier relationships and less burnout. ### **6. The skills you’re honing now (patience, multitasking, emotional intelligence) are assets in any role, whether you’re a CEO, an artist, or a stay-at-home parent.
